strengths: The paper addresses a useful, underexplored vision task: editing images to evoke a target emotion using only an image and an emotion category. Several qualitative examples demonstrate changes beyond color or texture transfer.

EmoPair provides a potentially useful resource: 331,595 emotion-labeled InstructPix2Pix pairs and 6,949 additional generated pairs. The manuscript attributes the underlying datasets and models and describes its curation pipeline.

The randomized human comparisons provide evidence of practical value, with approximately 56% average preference for EmoEditor. Attention controls and a small in-lab follow-up strengthen the experimental effort.
The manuscript reports ethical oversight and participant compensation, acknowledges concrete failure cases, and discusses potential misuse. These improve transparency.
weaknesses: The main automatic evaluation is coupled to the method. The same emotion predictor P labels/filters training data, selects inference outputs, and supplies EMR/ESR scores. Table 1 shows EMR rising from 5.06% without the critic to 50.20% with it, making this dependence consequential. Baselines are not given an equivalent critic or generation budget despite EmoEditor allowing up to 20 editing iterations. Independent evaluators and comparisons with matched inference budgets are needed to establish the source of the improvement.

The claimed architectural and reasoning novelty is insufficiently established. The emotion encoder receives only a one-hot category, so its alignment loss regularizes a fixed embedding per emotion; this alone does not demonstrate image-specific human-like or neuro-symbolic reasoning. A comparison against InstructPix2Pix fine-tuned on EmoPair with ordinary emotion prompts would better isolate the contribution. The directly relevant Affective Image Filter [30] is discussed but not evaluated.

Human evidence does not establish clear superiority over the strongest baseline. Preference over LMS is 54% online and 49% in-lab (Fig. S6), without confidence intervals or analysis accounting for repeated participants and source images. Only 27% of online participants passed the controls, making uncertainty and precise retained-sample accounting particularly important. These results support some usefulness, but the broad superiority claims exceed the evidence.

Dataset quality and semantic preservation need stronger validation. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels from a predictor reporting 73% accuracy on EmoSet, without a human audit of the resulting pairs. Ranking generic instructions does not validate individual emotional transitions. ENRD and ESS measure pixel/edge agreement rather than preserved meaning, while examples such as the tiger becoming coastal rocks (Fig. S10) illustrate the distinction. Human evaluation assesses emotion preference but not preservation; within-valence and neutral-image generalization receive only qualitative support.

The training formulation is materially ambiguous. Section 3.2 defines the noised latent from the source image and never clearly introduces the paired target image into the denoising objective. As written, this describes source reconstruction rather than supervised editing. Clarifying the target/conditioning roles is necessary for technical assessment. Missing learning rate, batch size, training duration, encoder dimensions, and sampling settings further limit reproducibility.

Several definitions and reporting errors require correction, although they are secondary to the evaluation concerns above. ESR uses KL divergence from a soft distribution to a one-hot target, which is infinite without smoothing or a different argument order. The stated 417,000 trials contradict 417 participants times 100 trials. The ablation discussion also reverses Table 1's preservation results: removing either component lowers, rather than raises, ENRD and ESS.
